knowledge_points.statement: The Earth has a crust (oceanic and continental), mantle and core. Plates move because of convection currents in the mantle, ridge push and slab pull.

At a destructive margin the denser oceanic plate subducts under the continental plate. Friction causes earthquakes; the subducting plate melts, and rising magma forms explosive composite volcanoes. An ocean trench forms.
At a constructive margin plates move apart. Magma rises through the gap to form new crust and gentle shield volcanoes, e.g. along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
At a conservative margin plates slide past each other. They stick, pressure builds and is released suddenly as an earthquake. There are no volcanoes.
People live in tectonic areas because of fertile volcanic soils, geothermal energy, tourism, minerals, family ties and jobs, and because some cannot afford to move.
Primary effects are caused directly by the hazard (ground shaking, collapsed buildings). Secondary effects result from the primary effects (fires, tsunamis, landslides, disease, job losses).

Immediate responses happen in the hours and days after a hazard (rescue, medical care, shelter, aid). Long-term responses happen over months and years (rebuilding, improving building codes, restoring the economy).

Effects are usually worse in lower-income countries: weaker buildings, less healthcare, fewer emergency services, less monitoring and education, and less money to rebuild. Higher-income countries usually have fewer deaths but higher economic costs.

Case studies: Nepal 2015 (magnitude 7.8, about 9,000 deaths, Kathmandu badly damaged, landslides blocked roads, avalanches on Everest, international aid). Chile 2010 (magnitude 8.8, about 500 deaths, tsunami, Concepción damaged, quick government response). Teacher to check figures.
Monitoring and prediction: seismometers, tiltmeters and GPS detect ground movement; gas sensors detect rising sulphur dioxide. These give warnings so people can evacuate.

Protection: earthquake-resistant buildings (cross-bracing, steel frames, rubber shock absorbers in the foundations, counterweights). Planning: hazard maps, land-use zoning, evacuation routes and earthquake drills.
Describing a relationship from data: state the trend (positive or negative), then support it with paired figures from the source, and note any anomaly.

Global atmospheric circulation: air rises at the equator (low pressure, heavy rain) and sinks at about 30° N and S (high pressure, dry). Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells; surface trade winds blow towards the equator.
Tropical storms form over oceans of at least 26–27°C, between about 5° and 30° from the equator, in late summer and autumn, where winds are light enough for the storm to build.

Formation: warm, moist air rises quickly, creating low pressure. Air rushes in, rises, cools and condenses into towering cumulonimbus clouds. Condensation releases heat (latent heat), which powers the storm. The Coriolis effect makes it spin. Cool air sinks in the centre, forming the eye.
The Coriolis effect is caused by the Earth's rotation. It is too weak near the equator (within about 5°), so storms cannot spin there.
Structure: the eye is calm, clear and has the lowest pressure (sinking air); the eyewall has the strongest winds and heaviest rain; spiral rain bands surround it.
Storms weaken over land or cooler water because they lose their supply of warm, moist air (their energy source), and friction with the land slows the winds.

Primary effects: strong winds, storm surge and coastal flooding, heavy rain and river flooding, landslides. Secondary effects: disease from dirty water, shortages of food and clean water, job losses, damage to the economy.

Reducing effects: monitoring (satellites, aircraft) and prediction of the storm's path; planning (evacuation routes, storm shelters, education); protection (sea walls, buildings on stilts, storm shutters, hurricane straps).

Climate change and storms: warmer oceans may make storms more intense (more category 4–5 storms), spread their formation further from the equator, and bring more rainfall; rising sea levels make storm surges worse. Changes in frequency are uncertain.

Typhoon Haiyan, Philippines, November 2013: winds over 300 km/h, storm surge of about 5 m, about 6,300 deaths, Tacloban badly hit, about 4 million people displaced, international aid. Teacher to check figures.
Describing a relationship between two variables on a graph: state the direction of the relationship and use paired data (with units) from the graph.
Weathering breaks down rock in place. Freeze-thaw: water in cracks freezes, expands by about 9%, and widens the crack. Carbonation: rainwater (a weak carbonic acid) dissolves limestone and chalk.
Mass movement is the downhill movement of material under gravity: sliding, slumping (rotational movement of saturated clay) and rockfall.

Coastal erosion: hydraulic action (force of water and compressed air in cracks), abrasion (rocks thrown at the cliff wear it away), attrition (rocks knock together and become smaller and rounder), solution (chemical dissolving of rock such as chalk).

Destructive waves: tall, steep, frequent (about 10–14 a minute), with a backwash stronger than the swash; they erode and remove beach material. Constructive waves: low, long, less frequent (about 6–8 a minute), with a swash stronger than the backwash; they build beaches.

Longshore drift: the prevailing wind makes waves approach at an angle; the swash carries sediment up the beach at that angle; the backwash returns it straight down the beach under gravity; this zigzag moves sediment along the coast.
Transport: traction (rolling), saltation (bouncing), suspension (carried in the water), solution (dissolved). Deposition happens where waves lose energy, e.g. sheltered bays.

Headlands and bays form on discordant coasts (alternating bands of hard and soft rock at right angles to the coast). Soft rock (e.g. clay) erodes faster to form bays; hard rock (e.g. chalk, granite) is resistant and is left as headlands.

Wave-cut platforms: waves erode the base of the cliff between high and low tide, forming a wave-cut notch. The cliff above becomes unsupported and collapses. Repeated, the cliff retreats, leaving a flat rocky platform exposed at low tide.

Cave, arch, stack, stump: hydraulic action and abrasion widen a crack in a headland into a cave; the cave erodes through the headland to form an arch; weathering and erosion weaken the arch roof until it collapses, leaving a stack; the stack is eroded at its base to form a stump.

Sand beaches have a gentle slope because small grains pack together, water drains slowly and the backwash carries sand back down. Shingle beaches are steep because water drains quickly through large pebbles, so the backwash is weak.

Spits form where the coastline changes direction: longshore drift carries sediment past the bend and deposits it in the sea, building a ridge. Changes in wind and wave direction curve the end (recurved end). Sheltered water behind forms salt marsh. A bar forms if a spit grows across a bay, trapping a lagoon.
Using rock type data: soft or unconsolidated rocks (clay, boulder clay) erode fastest; resistant rocks (granite, chalk, limestone) erode slowly.

Long and cross profile: the upper course is steep, with a narrow, shallow channel in a steep-sided V-shaped valley; the lower course has a gentle gradient, a wide, deep channel and a wide, flat valley floor (floodplain).

River erosion: hydraulic action (force of water), abrasion (rocks carried by the river scrape the bed and banks), attrition (rocks knock together, becoming smaller and rounder), solution (rock dissolved). Vertical erosion deepens the channel (upper course); lateral erosion widens it (middle and lower course).
Transport: traction (large boulders rolled along the bed), saltation (pebbles bounced), suspension (fine sediment carried in the water), solution (dissolved minerals).
Deposition happens when a river loses energy and slows down: on the inside of bends, when the river floods onto the floodplain, and at the mouth.
Interlocking spurs: in the upper course the river erodes vertically rather than laterally, and winds around ridges of more resistant rock, which interlock like a zip.

Waterfalls: a band of hard rock lies over softer rock. The soft rock is eroded faster (undercut) by hydraulic action and abrasion, forming a plunge pool and leaving an overhang of hard rock, which collapses. The waterfall retreats upstream, leaving a gorge.

Meanders: the fastest flow is on the outside of the bend, causing lateral erosion and a river cliff; slower flow on the inside causes deposition and a slip-off slope. A corkscrew (helicoidal) flow carries eroded material to the inside of the next bend.

Ox-bow lakes: erosion on the outside of two bends narrows the neck of a meander. During a flood the river cuts through the neck, taking the straighter, shorter route. Deposition seals off the old meander, leaving an ox-bow lake.

Floodplains and levees: when a river floods, water spreads out, slows and deposits sediment. The heaviest, coarsest material is dropped first, next to the channel, building levees; finer silt is carried further, building up the floodplain. Meanders migrating sideways widen the floodplain.

Downstream, discharge, channel width, depth and velocity usually increase. Velocity increases because the channel is more efficient: a smaller proportion of the water touches the bed and banks, so there is less friction.

River landforms case study, e.g. the River Tees: High Force waterfall (hard whinstone over softer limestone and shale) and a gorge in the upper course; meanders and ox-bow lakes near Yarm and Stockton in the lower course; estuary with mudflats at Teesmouth. Teacher to check details.
Cross-sectional area = width × mean depth. Discharge = cross-sectional area × velocity (cumecs).

activities.title: Two kinds of wave
activities.body:
**Destructive waves** are tall, steep and frequent (10–14 a minute). Their **backwash** is stronger than their swash, so they **remove** material and erode.

**Constructive waves** are low and gentle (6–8 a minute). Their **swash** is stronger, so they **build up** beaches.

activities.prompt: Why do constructive waves build up beaches?
options: Their swash is stronger than their backwash
explanations: Correct: more material is carried up the beach than dragged back.

activities.title: Four ways the sea erodes
activities.body:
**Hydraulic action:** water and trapped air are forced into cracks, breaking the rock.
**Abrasion:** rocks thrown by waves wear away the cliff.
**Attrition:** rocks knock into each other and become smaller and rounder.
**Solution:** sea water dissolves rocks such as chalk and limestone.

activities.text: When rocks carried by waves knock into each other and become smaller and rounder, this is called ___ .
activities.answer: attrition

activities.title: Weathering and mass movement
activities.body:
**Weathering** breaks rock down where it is. In **freeze-thaw**, water in cracks freezes, expands and widens the crack. In **carbonation**, slightly acidic rain dissolves chalk and limestone.

**Mass movement** is material moving downhill under gravity: **rockfalls**, **sliding**, and **slumping** of wet clay cliffs.

activities.prompt: Which of these is weathering, not erosion?
explanations: Correct: rock broken down in place by freezing water.
Erosion: rocks wearing each other down.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between abrasion and attrition?
activities.answer: Abrasion: rocks carried by waves wear away the cliff or bed. Attrition: rocks knock into each other and get smaller and rounder.

activities.title: Headlands and bays
activities.body: Where bands of **hard and soft rock** meet the coast, the **soft rock** (like clay) erodes quickly to form **bays**. The **hard rock** (like chalk or granite) resists and sticks out as **headlands**. Bays become sheltered, so beaches often form in them.

activities.title: Wave-cut platforms
activities.body: Waves attack the **foot of a cliff** between high and low tide, cutting a **wave-cut notch**. The cliff above is left **overhanging** and eventually **collapses**. This repeats, so the cliff **retreats**, leaving a flat, rocky **wave-cut platform** that shows at low tide.

activities.prompt: Put the formation of a wave-cut platform in order.
steps: Waves erode the foot of the cliff
A wave-cut notch forms
The cliff above overhangs
The overhang collapses
The cliff retreats, leaving a flat platform

activities.title: Cave, arch, stack, stump
activities.body: Waves attack a **crack** in a headland by hydraulic action and abrasion. The crack grows into a **cave**. The cave erodes right through to form an **arch**. Weathering and erosion weaken the arch roof until it **collapses**, leaving a **stack**. The stack is eroded at its base until it becomes a **stump**.

activities.prompt: Put these landforms in the order they form.
steps: Crack
Cave
Arch
Stack
Stump

activities.prompt: What turns an arch into a stack?
explanations: Correct: weathering and erosion weaken the roof until it falls.
Longshore drift moves sediment, not headlands.
Tides don't remove arches by themselves.

activities.title: Longshore drift
activities.body: The **prevailing wind** makes waves approach the beach **at an angle**. The **swash** carries sediment up the beach at that angle. The **backwash** carries it **straight back down** because of gravity. Repeated, this **zigzag** moves sediment along the coast.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of longshore drift in order.
steps: The prevailing wind drives waves in at an angle
The swash carries sediment up the beach at an angle
The backwash carries it straight back down
The zigzag repeats, moving sediment along the coast

activities.title: Beaches
activities.body: Sediment is **deposited** where waves lose energy, such as in sheltered bays. **Sand beaches** are gently sloping: the small grains pack tightly, water drains slowly and the backwash pulls sand back down. **Shingle beaches** are steep: water drains quickly through big pebbles, so the backwash is weak.

activities.title: Spits and bars
activities.body: Where the coast **changes direction**, longshore drift carries sediment on into the sea. In the sheltered water it's **deposited**, building a long ridge: a **spit**. Changing winds curve its end into a **hook**. Calm water behind it lets **salt marsh** form. If a spit grows right across a bay, it becomes a **bar** with a **lagoon** behind.

activities.prompt: Why does a spit form where the coastline changes direction?
options: Longshore drift carries sediment on into calmer water, where it is deposited
Rivers always meet the sea there
explanations: Correct: deposition builds the ridge out from the bend.
A river may be present but isn't the cause.

activities.text: If a spit grows right across a bay, it forms a ___ with a lagoon behind it.
activities.answer: bar

activities.title: Using rock type data
activities.body: When a figure shows **rock type**, use it. Soft or loose rocks such as **clay** and **boulder clay** erode fastest. Resistant rocks such as **granite**, chalk and limestone erode slowly. Always quote numbers with **units**: '2.4 m per year', not just '2.4'.

activities.title: How to write a 6-mark 'explain' answer
activities.body:
1. Go in **order**: what happens first, next, last.
2. **Name the processes** (hydraulic action, abrasion, deposition).
3. Link with **'so' and 'because'**: each step should explain why the next happens.
4. Use the **figure** if there is one: directions, place names, labels.

activities.title: From source to mouth
activities.body:
In the **upper course** the land is steep. The channel is narrow and shallow, in a steep-sided **V-shaped valley**.

In the **lower course** the gradient is gentle. The channel is **wide and deep**, and the valley has a wide, flat floor: the **floodplain**.

activities.title: River erosion
activities.body:
**Hydraulic action:** the force of the water. **Abrasion:** rocks carried by the river scrape the bed and banks. **Attrition:** rocks knock together and become smaller and rounder. **Solution:** rock dissolves.

**Vertical erosion** deepens the channel (upper course). **Lateral erosion** widens it (lower down).

activities.prompt: Which kind of erosion is most important in the upper course?
explanations: Lateral erosion dominates lower down, forming meanders.
Correct: the river cuts downwards, forming V-shaped valleys.

activities.title: Transport and deposition
activities.body:
Rivers carry their load by **traction** (big boulders rolled), **saltation** (pebbles bounced), **suspension** (fine sediment carried) and **solution** (dissolved).

When a river **slows down** it loses energy and **deposits** its load: on the inside of bends, on the floodplain in floods, and at the mouth.

activities.text: Pebbles bouncing along the river bed are being moved by ___ .
activities.answer: saltation

activities.title: Faster downstream?
activities.body: Surprisingly, rivers usually flow **faster downstream** even though the land is flatter. The channel gets **wider, deeper and smoother**, so less of the water touches the bed and banks: there's **less friction**. Tributaries also add more water.

activities.prompt: Why does a river's velocity usually increase downstream?
activities.answer: The channel is wider, deeper and smoother, so a smaller proportion of the water touches the bed and banks: less friction. Tributaries also add water.

activities.title: Interlocking spurs
activities.body: In the upper course the river mainly erodes **downwards**. It doesn't have the energy to cut sideways through hard rock, so it **winds around** it. This leaves ridges of land, called **spurs**, that **interlock** from either side of the valley, like the teeth of a zip.

activities.title: Waterfalls and gorges
activities.body: A waterfall forms where **hard rock lies on top of softer rock**. The soft rock erodes faster, **undercutting** the hard rock and forming a deep **plunge pool**. The hard rock is left as an **overhang**, which **collapses**. As this repeats, the waterfall **moves back upstream**, leaving a steep-sided **gorge**.

activities.prompt: Put the formation of a waterfall in order.
steps: Hard rock lies on top of softer rock
The soft rock is eroded faster and undercut
A plunge pool forms and an overhang is left
The overhang collapses
The waterfall retreats upstream, forming a gorge

activities.prompt: Why does a gorge form downstream of a waterfall?
options: Deposition builds up the valley sides
The waterfall retreats upstream as overhangs collapse
explanations: Correct: each collapse moves the falls back, leaving a gorge.

activities.prompt: Why does the river wind around spurs instead of cutting through them?
activities.answer: In the upper course it mainly erodes vertically and doesn't have enough energy to erode sideways through the hard rock.

activities.title: Meanders
activities.body: On a bend, the **fastest flow** swings to the **outside**. It erodes sideways, forming a steep **river cliff**. On the **inside**, the water is slow and shallow, so it **deposits** sediment, forming a gentle **slip-off slope**. Over time the bends grow bigger.

activities.prompt: Where on a meander is a river cliff found?
options: On the inside of the bend
On the outside of the bend
In the middle of the channel
explanations: The inside has slow water and deposition: a slip-off slope.
Correct: the fastest flow erodes the outside bank.

activities.title: Ox-bow lakes
activities.body: Erosion on the outside of two bends **narrows the neck** of land between them. In a **flood**, the river **cuts through the neck**, taking the shortest route. **Deposition** seals off the old loop, leaving a horseshoe-shaped **ox-bow lake**.

activities.prompt: Put the formation of an ox-bow lake in order.
steps: Erosion on the outside of bends narrows the neck
During a flood the river cuts through the neck
The river takes the new, straighter route
Deposition seals off the old meander
An ox-bow lake is left

activities.title: Floodplains and levees
activities.body: When a river **floods**, the water spreads out, slows and **deposits** sediment. The **heaviest** material drops first, right next to the channel. Many floods build it up into raised banks: **levees**. Finer silt spreads further, building the flat **floodplain**.

activities.text: Raised banks of sediment along the edge of a river are called ___ .
activities.answer: levees

activities.title: River calculations
activities.body:
**Cross-sectional area** = width × mean depth (m²).
**Discharge** = cross-sectional area × velocity (m³/s, called **cumecs**).
Example: width 8 m, depth 0.5 m: area = **4 m²**. At 0.6 m/s, discharge = **2.4 cumecs**.

activities.title: Case study: River Tees
activities.body:
**Upper course:** **High Force**, a waterfall about 21 m high, where hard **whinstone** lies over softer limestone and shale, with a gorge below it.
**Lower course:** large **meanders** near **Yarm**, ox-bow lakes near **Stockton**, a floodplain and levees.
**Mouth:** the **estuary** at Teesmouth, with mudflats.

activities.prompt: Name one upper-course and one lower-course landform on the River Tees, with places.
activities.answer: Upper: High Force waterfall (whinstone over limestone) and its gorge. Lower: meanders near Yarm; ox-bow lakes near Stockton; estuary at Teesmouth.

activities.title: Global atmospheric circulation
activities.body: The sun heats the **equator** most. Warm air **rises** there, creating **low pressure**, clouds and heavy rain. At about **30° north and south** the air **sinks**, creating **high pressure** and dry weather: that's where most hot deserts are. These loops of air are called **cells** (Hadley, Ferrel and Polar).

activities.prompt: What happens to air at about 30° north and south of the equator?
explanations: Rising air and low pressure are at the equator.
Correct: sinking air gives high pressure and dry conditions.
Air is always moving in the cells.

activities.title: Winds at the surface
activities.body: Air moves at the surface from **high pressure to low pressure**. So surface winds blow from 30° back towards the equator: these are the **trade winds**. They blow from the east, which is why tropical storms usually travel **westwards** across the oceans.

activities.text: At the equator, warm air rises, creating an area of ___ pressure.
activities.answer: low

activities.prompt: Why are many hot deserts found at about 30° north and south?
activities.answer: Air sinks there, creating high pressure, so clouds and rain rarely form.

activities.title: The right conditions
activities.body:
Tropical storms need:
• ocean water of at least **27°C**
• a location between about **5° and 30°** from the equator
• light winds high up, so the storm can grow tall

That's why they mostly form in **late summer and autumn**, when the sea is warmest.

activities.title: Building a storm
activities.body: **Warm, moist air rises** quickly from the sea, leaving **low pressure** below. More air rushes in and rises. As it rises it **cools and condenses** into towering clouds, and condensation **releases heat**, which makes the air rise even faster. The **Coriolis effect**, from the Earth's spin, makes the storm **rotate**. It's too weak at the equator, so storms can't form there.

activities.prompt: Put the stages of storm formation in order.
steps: The sea is heated to over 27°C
Warm, moist air rises quickly
Low pressure forms and more air is drawn in
Rising air cools and condenses into huge clouds
Released heat powers the storm and the Coriolis effect makes it spin

activities.prompt: Why don't tropical storms form right on the equator?
options: The Coriolis effect is too weak to make them spin
explanations: The sea at the equator is warm.
Correct: no spin, no organised storm.
Air does rise strongly at the equator.

activities.title: Inside the storm
activities.body: The **eye** is the calm centre: clear skies, light winds and the **lowest pressure**, because air is sinking. Around it, the **eyewall** has the **strongest winds** and **heaviest rain**. Further out, **spiral rain bands** bring more bursts of rain.

activities.text: The strongest winds and heaviest rain are found in the ___ .
activities.answer: eyewall

activities.title: What storms do
activities.body:
**Primary effects:** strong winds destroy buildings and power lines; a **storm surge** (a wall of sea water pushed ashore) floods the coast; heavy rain causes flooding and landslides.

**Secondary effects:** disease from dirty water, shortages of food and clean water, lost jobs and damage to the economy.

activities.prompt: What is a storm surge?
options: A rise in sea level pushed onto the coast by the storm's winds and low pressure
A sudden change in wind direction
explanations: Heavy rain is a separate effect.
Correct: and it is often the deadliest effect.

activities.title: Why storms die
activities.body: Over land, a storm is cut off from the **warm sea**, its energy source. Less water vapour condenses, so less heat is released, and **friction** with hills and buildings slows the winds. That's why storms weaken quickly after **landfall**.

activities.title: Reducing the effects
activities.body:
**Monitoring and prediction:** satellites and aircraft track storms, so warnings can be given days ahead.
**Planning:** evacuation routes, storm shelters, drills and emergency supplies.
**Protection:** sea walls, homes on stilts, storm shutters and strengthened roofs.

activities.prompt: Which of these is protection, not planning?
explanations: Correct: it changes the building to resist the hazard.

activities.prompt: Why do tropical storms lose strength over land?
activities.answer: They lose their supply of warm, moist air from the sea (their energy), and friction with the land slows the winds.

activities.title: Case study: Typhoon Haiyan
activities.body: **Philippines, November 2013.** Winds over 300 km/h and a **storm surge of about 5 m**. About **6,300 deaths**; the city of **Tacloban** was devastated; about 4 million people displaced. About 800,000 people were evacuated, but some shelters flooded. International aid arrived, but damaged airports and roads slowed it.

activities.prompt: Give two specific facts about Typhoon Haiyan.
activities.answer: Any two: Philippines, November 2013; winds over 300 km/h; storm surge about 5 m; about 6,300 deaths; Tacloban devastated; about 4 million displaced.

activities.title: Storms in a warmer world
activities.body: Warmer oceans give storms **more energy**, so more may reach **category 4 or 5**. More of the ocean will be above 27°C, so storms may reach **new areas**. Warmer air holds **more moisture**, so more rain. Rising seas make **storm surges worse**. Whether there will be more storms overall is **uncertain**.

activities.title: The Earth's layers
activities.body: The Earth has a thin rocky **crust**, a hot **mantle** and a **core**. The crust is broken into huge pieces called **plates**. Oceanic crust is thin and dense; continental crust is thicker and lighter. Plates move a few centimetres a year, pushed and pulled by **convection currents** in the mantle, ridge push and slab pull.

activities.prompt: Which type of crust is denser?
options: Neither: only the mantle has density
explanations: Continental crust is thicker but lighter.
Correct: oceanic crust is thinner and denser, which is why it sinks.
They differ, and that difference matters at destructive margins.
All rock has density; oceanic crust is the denser crust.

activities.title: Destructive margins
activities.body: At a **destructive margin** an oceanic plate moves towards a continental plate. The denser oceanic plate is **subducted** (sinks) under the continental plate, forming a deep **ocean trench**. Friction causes **earthquakes**. The sinking plate **melts** in the mantle, and the magma rises to form explosive **composite volcanoes**.

activities.prompt: Put the events at a destructive margin in order.
steps: Oceanic and continental plates move towards each other
The denser oceanic plate is subducted
The sinking plate melts in the mantle
Magma rises through cracks in the crust
An explosive volcano erupts

activities.title: Constructive and conservative margins
activities.body:
At a **constructive margin** plates move **apart**. Magma rises to fill the gap, forming new crust and gentle **shield volcanoes**, as in Iceland on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

At a **conservative margin** plates **slide past** each other. They stick, pressure builds, then they jolt: an **earthquake**. No magma rises, so there are **no volcanoes**.

activities.prompt: Why are there no volcanoes at conservative margins?
options: No crust is destroyed and no gap opens, so magma cannot rise
explanations: Correct: with no subduction and no gap, there is no route for magma.
Earthquakes don't prevent volcanoes; destructive margins have both.

activities.text: At a constructive margin the plates move ___ and magma rises to fill the gap.
activities.answer: apart

activities.prompt: Why does the oceanic plate sink at a destructive margin?
activities.answer: Because it is denser than the continental plate.

activities.title: Primary and secondary effects
activities.body:
**Primary effects** are caused directly by the hazard: ground shaking, collapsed buildings, people killed by falling rubble.

**Secondary effects** happen as a result of the primary effects: fires from broken gas pipes, tsunamis, landslides, disease from dirty water, people losing their jobs.

activities.prompt: Which is a secondary effect of an earthquake?
explanations: Correct: this follows from damage to water and sewage pipes.

activities.title: Immediate and long-term responses
activities.body:
**Immediate responses** happen in the hours and days after: search and rescue, medical care, emergency shelter, food and water, aid from other countries.

**Long-term responses** happen over months and years: rebuilding homes and roads, stronger building rules, restoring jobs and the economy.

activities.text: Rebuilding homes to stricter building codes is a ___ response.
activities.answer: long-term

activities.title: Why wealth matters
activities.body:
The same size of earthquake usually kills **more people in low-income countries**. Buildings are weaker, there are fewer hospitals and rescue teams, less monitoring and fewer drills, and less money to rebuild.

High-income countries usually have **fewer deaths** but **higher economic costs**, because their buildings and infrastructure are worth more.

activities.prompt: Give two reasons why earthquakes kill more people in low-income countries.
activities.answer: Any two: weaker buildings that collapse; fewer hospitals and emergency services; less monitoring, education and drills; poor roads that slow rescue.

activities.title: Why live near danger?
activities.body: Millions of people live near volcanoes and fault lines. Volcanic soils are **fertile**, so farming is good. **Geothermal energy** gives cheap power. Volcanoes attract **tourists**, bringing jobs. Some areas have valuable **minerals**. Many people have family and jobs there, or simply **cannot afford to move**.

activities.prompt: Why are the soils around volcanoes good for farming?
options: Volcanic ash and rock weather into soil rich in minerals
explanations: Lava destroys farmland rather than warming it.
Correct: weathered volcanic material is full of nutrients.
Volcanoes don't make soils fertile through rain.

activities.title: Monitoring and prediction
activities.body: Earthquakes can't yet be predicted, but volcanoes give warning signs. **Seismometers** detect small earthquakes as magma rises. **Tiltmeters** and **GPS** spot the ground swelling. **Gas sensors** detect more sulphur dioxide. These signs give time to **evacuate**.

activities.text: A ___ detects the small earthquakes that happen as magma rises inside a volcano.
activities.answer: seismometer

activities.title: Protection and planning
activities.body:
**Protection** means designing buildings to survive: steel **cross-bracing**, **rubber shock absorbers** in the foundations, **counterweights** on the roof.

**Planning** keeps people safe and is cheaper: **hazard maps**, keeping homes and hospitals out of the riskiest zones, evacuation routes and **earthquake drills**.

activities.prompt: Which of these is protection rather than planning?
options: Rubber shock absorbers in a building's foundations
explanations: Hazard maps are planning: deciding where to build.
Correct: protection changes the building itself.

activities.prompt: Name the three Ps of reducing tectonic risk (alongside monitoring).
activities.answer: Prediction, protection and planning (with monitoring).

activities.title: Two earthquakes compared
activities.body:
**Nepal, 2015** (low income): magnitude 7.8, about **9,000 deaths**. Many homes of brick and stone collapsed; landslides blocked roads, slowing aid.

**Chile, 2010** (higher income): magnitude 8.8, **stronger**, yet about **500 deaths**. Strict building codes and a fast government response, though a tsunami hit the coast.

activities.prompt: Chile's 2010 earthquake was stronger than Nepal's in 2015, yet killed far fewer people. What is the best explanation?
options: Chile has strict building codes and better emergency services
Nepal is closer to a plate margin
explanations: Correct: development affects building quality and response.
Population size isn't the main reason.

exam_questions.stem: Explain why volcanoes form at both destructive and constructive plate margins.

papers_consulted: OCR B J259/01 Our Natural World June 2024 QP

exam_questions.model_answer:
At a destructive plate margin an oceanic plate moves towards a continental plate. The oceanic plate is denser, so it is subducted beneath the continental plate. As it sinks into the mantle, heat and friction cause it to melt, forming magma. This magma is less dense than the rock around it, so it rises through cracks in the crust and erupts at the surface. Because the magma is thick and full of gas, the eruptions are explosive and build steep composite volcanoes.

At a constructive margin the two plates move apart, pulled by convection currents in the mantle. As they separate, the pressure is reduced and magma rises up from the mantle to fill the gap. The lava is runny, so it flows a long way before cooling, building wide shield volcanoes with gentle slopes, such as those in Iceland on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. In both cases volcanoes form because magma is able to reach the surface where the plates meet or separate.

exam_questions.stem: 'Protection is the most effective way to reduce the risk from tectonic hazards.' How far do you agree? Give reasons for your view.

papers_consulted: OCR B J259/01 Our Natural World June 2024 QP

exam_questions.model_answer:
I partly agree. Protection is very effective for earthquakes because most deaths are caused by buildings collapsing. Buildings with rubber shock absorbers in their foundations and steel cross-bracing can sway without falling down, which protects people even though earthquakes cannot be predicted. However, protection is expensive, so it is less realistic in low-income countries where many people live in poorly built homes, and it does little against lava flows or ash from a volcano.

For volcanoes, monitoring is often more effective. Seismometers, tiltmeters and gas sensors can detect signs that magma is rising, so people can be evacuated before an eruption. Planning is also important and cheap: hazard maps can stop people building in the most dangerous zones, and earthquake drills teach people to drop, cover and hold on.

Overall, protection is the most effective way to reduce earthquake risk in richer countries, but for volcanoes and in poorer countries, monitoring and planning save more lives. The best approach is to combine all three.

exam_questions.stem: 'The effects of a tectonic hazard depend mainly on the level of development of the country where it happens.' Use named examples to assess this statement.

papers_consulted: OCR B J259/01 Our Natural World June 2024 QP

exam_questions.model_answer:
Level of development has a big influence on the effects of tectonic hazards. The 2015 earthquake in Nepal, a low-income country, had a magnitude of 7.8 and killed nearly 9,000 people. Many homes in rural areas were built of mud brick and stone and collapsed, and landslides blocked roads so rescue teams and aid struggled to reach remote villages. Nepal relied heavily on international aid, such as helicopters from India, because it had few resources of its own.

In contrast, the 2010 earthquake in Chile, a richer country, was much stronger at magnitude 8.8, yet about 500 people died. Chile has strict building codes, so most modern buildings stayed standing, and the government's emergency services responded quickly, restoring power and water to most people within days. This suggests development reduces deaths even when the hazard is stronger.

However, development is not the only factor. Physical factors matter: Chile's earthquake caused a tsunami, which caused many of its deaths, and Nepal's steep mountain slopes made landslides worse. The depth of the earthquake and how close it is to large cities also affect the damage. Richer countries may also suffer greater economic effects: Chile's damage cost around 30 billion US dollars because there was more valuable property and infrastructure.

Overall, I mostly agree. Level of development is the main factor in how many people die, because it controls building quality and the speed of the response. But the size and location of the hazard and secondary hazards also matter, and economic losses are often higher in richer countries.

exam_questions.stem: Explain how global atmospheric circulation helps to explain where tropical storms form.

papers_consulted: OCR B J259/01 Our Natural World June 2024 QP

exam_questions.model_answer:
At the equator the sun's heating is most intense. Warm air rises, creating a belt of low pressure where the two Hadley cells meet. This rising, warm, moist air is what tropical storms need, and the oceans here are heated to over 27°C. However, storms do not form right on the equator because the Coriolis effect is too weak to make the air spin, so they form between about 5° and 30° from the equator.

At around 30° north and south, air in the Hadley cells sinks, creating high pressure. Sinking air stops clouds from forming, and the oceans beyond this latitude are cooler, so storms rarely form there.

The trade winds, which blow from the high pressure at 30° towards the low pressure at the equator, steer storms westwards across the oceans, which is why places like the Caribbean and the Philippines are often hit. The low-pressure belt also moves north and south with the seasons, so storms form in late summer and autumn when the sea is warmest.

exam_questions.stem: 'Planning is more important than protection in reducing the effects of tropical storms.' How far do you agree? Give reasons for your view.

papers_consulted: OCR B J259/01 Our Natural World June 2024 QP

exam_questions.model_answer:
I mostly agree. Planning saves the most lives. Evacuation routes, storm shelters and education mean that when a warning is given, people know where to go and what to do. In Bangladesh, cyclone shelters and warning systems have greatly reduced deaths compared with the past. Planning is also fairly cheap, so it is realistic for low-income countries.

However, protection is important for reducing damage to homes and infrastructure. Sea walls and storm surge barriers can stop flooding, and building homes on stilts or adding storm shutters reduces damage. But protection is expensive and can fail if a storm is stronger than expected; in New Orleans in 2005 some levees failed, flooding much of the city.

Overall, planning is more important because it reduces deaths, which are the most serious effect. Protection reduces economic losses, so in richer countries both should be used together.

exam_questions.stem: For a named tropical storm, evaluate how effective the immediate and long-term responses were.

papers_consulted: OCR B J259/01 Our Natural World June 2024 QP

exam_questions.model_answer:
Typhoon Haiyan hit the Philippines in November 2013 with winds of over 300 km/h and a storm surge of about 5 metres, killing around 6,300 people.

The immediate responses were partly effective. Around 800,000 people were evacuated before the typhoon arrived, which saved many lives. However, some people sheltered in buildings such as schools and churches that were flooded by the storm surge, because the warnings did not explain clearly what a storm surge was. International aid arrived quickly from countries such as the UK and the USA, including food, water, shelter and field hospitals. But damaged airports and blocked roads meant aid took days or even weeks to reach remote islands, and in Tacloban there was looting because people were desperate for food.

The long-term responses were more effective at reducing future risk. The government planned to 'build back better', making homes and schools stronger, and created no-build zones near the coast. Mangroves were replanted to absorb future storm surges, and cash-for-work schemes paid people to clear debris, helping them earn money. However, rebuilding was slow, and some families moved away from the coast were far from their fishing jobs.

Overall, the immediate responses saved many lives through evacuation but were limited by poor communication and damaged transport. The long-term responses were more effective because they reduced the risk from future typhoons, even though progress was slow. The responses were held back by the Philippines' level of development and the huge scale of the damage.

exam_questions.stem: Describe the process of longshore drift.
exam_questions.model_answer: Waves approach the coast at an angle because of the prevailing wind. The swash carries sand and pebbles up the beach at this angle. The backwash then carries them straight back down the beach because of gravity. This zigzag movement is repeated, so sediment is gradually transported along the coast.

exam_questions.stem: Explain the processes that create a wave-cut platform.
exam_questions.model_answer: Waves erode the foot of the cliff, in the zone between high tide and low tide, by hydraulic action and abrasion. This forms a wave-cut notch. As the notch gets deeper, the cliff above is left unsupported and eventually collapses. This happens again and again, so the cliff retreats inland, leaving behind a flat rocky wave-cut platform that is exposed at low tide.

exam_questions.stem: Explain one way in which weathering helps to form coastal landforms.
exam_questions.model_answer: Freeze-thaw weathering happens when water gets into cracks in the roof of an arch, freezes and expands, widening the cracks. Over time this weakens the roof until it collapses, leaving a stack.

exam_questions.stem: Explain why headlands and bays form on some coastlines.
exam_questions.model_answer: Headlands and bays form where bands of hard and soft rock meet the coast. The soft rock, such as clay, is eroded quickly by the waves and forms a bay. The hard rock, such as chalk, is more resistant, so it erodes slowly and is left sticking out into the sea as a headland.

exam_questions.stem: Explain why sandy beaches usually have a gentler slope than shingle (pebble) beaches.
exam_questions.model_answer: Sand grains are small and packed tightly together, so water drains into the beach slowly. This means the backwash stays strong and carries sand back down, spreading it out into a gentle slope. Water drains quickly through large pebbles, so the backwash on a shingle beach is weak and the pebbles pile up into a steep slope.

exam_questions.stem: Study the figure. Explain how the spit shown has formed.
exam_questions.model_answer:
The prevailing wind blows from the south-west, so waves approach the coast at an angle. Longshore drift moves sand and shingle eastwards: the swash carries sediment up the beach at an angle and the backwash carries it straight back down under gravity. Where the coastline turns sharply north into the estuary, the longshore drift continues in the same direction out into the sea. The water here is more sheltered, so the waves lose energy and deposit their sediment, building up a long, narrow ridge of sand and shingle.

Over time, changes in the wind and wave direction bend its tip round into the hook shown in the figure. The river flowing out of the estuary stops the spit growing all the way across. Behind the spit the water is calm and sheltered, so fine silt and mud settle, and plants colonise them to form the salt marsh.

exam_questions.stem: Explain how erosion and weathering lead to the formation of a stack.
exam_questions.model_answer:
Headlands are made of hard rock, but they have weaknesses such as cracks and joints. Waves attack these weaknesses by hydraulic action, forcing water and air into the cracks, and by abrasion, as rocks are thrown against the cliff. Over time the crack widens into a cave.

The cave continues to be eroded until it cuts right through the headland, forming an arch. The base of the arch is eroded by the waves, while the roof is weakened by weathering. For example, freeze-thaw weathering widens cracks when water freezes and expands, and in chalk or limestone, carbonation dissolves the rock. Eventually the roof of the arch becomes too weak to support itself and collapses under gravity. This leaves a tall pillar of rock separated from the headland, called a stack. Further erosion at its base may later turn it into a stump.

exam_questions.stem: 'Erosion is more important than deposition in shaping coastal landscapes.' How far do you agree? Give reasons for your view.
exam_questions.model_answer:
On rocky, high-energy coasts erosion is the most important process. Destructive waves erode cliffs by hydraulic action and abrasion, creating wave-cut platforms, headlands and bays, and caves, arches and stacks. These are the most dramatic coastal landforms.

However, on sheltered, low-energy coasts deposition is more important. Constructive waves build up beaches, and longshore drift carries sediment that is deposited to form spits and bars, while calm water behind spits allows salt marshes to form. Sand dunes also develop from deposited sand.

The two processes depend on each other: the sediment that forms beaches and spits mostly comes from cliffs that have been eroded, and bays formed by erosion become sheltered places for beaches. Overall, I partly agree: erosion is more important on rocky, exposed coasts, but deposition is more important on sheltered coasts, and both work together to shape most coastlines.

exam_questions.stem: Identify which one of these landforms is usually found in the upper course of a river.

explanations.A: Levees form in the lower course when rivers flood.
explanations.B: Ox-bow lakes form from meanders in the middle and lower course.

explanations.D: An estuary is at the river's mouth.

exam_questions.stem: Explain why a river's velocity usually increases downstream, even though its gradient becomes gentler.
exam_questions.model_answer: Downstream the channel becomes wider, deeper and smoother. This means a smaller proportion of the water is in contact with the bed and banks, so there is less friction to slow the water down and it flows faster.

exam_questions.stem: Define the term 'abrasion' in a river.
exam_questions.model_answer: Abrasion is when rocks and pebbles carried by the river scrape against the bed and banks, wearing them away.

exam_questions.stem: Study the figure. Explain why deposition happens at Y.
exam_questions.model_answer: Y is on the inside of the bend, where the water is shallower and flows more slowly because of friction. The river has less energy here, so it deposits sand and gravel, forming a slip-off slope.

exam_questions.stem: Explain how a waterfall and gorge are formed.
exam_questions.model_answer: Waterfalls form where a band of hard rock lies on top of softer rock. The soft rock is eroded faster by hydraulic action and abrasion, undercutting the hard rock and forming a plunge pool at the base. This leaves an overhang of hard rock, which becomes unsupported and collapses. As this happens again and again, the waterfall moves back upstream, cutting a steep-sided gorge.

exam_questions.stem: Describe how the cross profile of a river valley changes from the upper course to the lower course.
exam_questions.model_answer: In the upper course the valley is narrow and V-shaped with steep sides, and the channel is narrow and shallow. By the lower course the valley is wide, with gentle sides and a flat floodplain, and the channel is wide and deep.

exam_questions.stem: Explain how interlocking spurs are formed.
exam_questions.model_answer: In the upper course the river mainly erodes vertically, cutting downwards. It does not have enough energy to erode sideways through areas of hard rock, so it winds around them, leaving ridges of land that interlock from either side of the valley.

exam_questions.stem: Explain one difference between vertical and lateral erosion.
exam_questions.model_answer: Vertical erosion cuts downwards and deepens the river channel, while lateral erosion cuts sideways and widens it. Vertical erosion is most common in the upper course, where it forms V-shaped valleys, whereas lateral erosion is more common in the lower course, where it forms meanders.

exam_questions.stem: Explain how meanders and ox-bow lakes are formed.
exam_questions.model_answer:
As a river flows around a bend, the fastest flow swings to the outside, where the water is deeper and has more energy. Here lateral erosion by hydraulic action and abrasion undercuts the bank, forming a steep river cliff. On the inside of the bend the water is shallow and slow, so the river loses energy and deposits sediment, forming a gentle slip-off slope. A corkscrew-like flow carries eroded material from the outside of one bend to the inside of the next, so over time the bends become larger and more pronounced.

As erosion continues on the outside of two bends, the neck of land between them gets narrower. During a flood, when the river has extra energy, it cuts through the neck and takes the shorter, straighter route. Deposition then seals off the ends of the old meander loop, leaving a horseshoe-shaped ox-bow lake. Over time the lake may dry out, leaving a meander scar.

exam_questions.stem: Explain how floodplains and levees are formed.
exam_questions.model_answer:
Floodplains are wide, flat areas of land on either side of a river in its lower course. They are formed partly by lateral erosion, as meanders migrate across the valley and widen it. When the river floods, water spreads out over this land. Because it is shallower and meets more friction, it slows down and loses energy, depositing a layer of sediment called alluvium. Over many floods these layers build up into a flat floodplain.

Levees form at the same time. As soon as the river overflows its banks, the water slows down sharply, so the heaviest and coarsest sediment is dropped first, right next to the channel. Finer silt and clay are carried further across the floodplain before being deposited. After repeated floods, the coarse material builds up into raised banks along the edge of the river called levees.

exam_questions.stem: For a named river, describe and explain the landforms found along its course.
exam_questions.model_answer:
The River Tees flows from the Pennines to the North Sea. In its upper course there is High Force, a waterfall about 21 metres high. It formed where a layer of hard whinstone lies on top of softer limestone and shale. The softer rock is eroded faster by hydraulic action and abrasion, undercutting the whinstone, which collapses. As this repeats, the waterfall has retreated upstream, leaving a steep-sided gorge. The river here mostly erodes vertically, so the valley is V-shaped with interlocking spurs.

In the lower course, near Yarm, the river forms large meanders. Lateral erosion on the outside of bends forms river cliffs, and deposition on the inside forms slip-off slopes. Near Stockton some meanders have been cut off to form ox-bow lakes. The river also has a wide floodplain with levees, formed when floodwater slows and deposits sediment. Finally, at Teesmouth there is an estuary, where the river meets the sea and deposits mud, forming mudflats and salt marsh.
